newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel IPO delayed by London market nerves.
newsitem.headline: Israel IPO delayed by London market nerves.

text.p: Clashes between Israelis and Palestinians claimed their first stock market casualty on Thursday when a five million pound ($7.6 million) London initial public offering in Israel's Nechustan Metals was postponed.

Nechustan's parent company Nechustan Investments announced that the IPO, slated for November for 30 percent of equity, would be put off until early 1997 at the recommendation of its London financial adviser Dawnay Day.
Nechustan chairman Levi Kushnir blamed the delay on political events.
"We discussed the offering last week and Dawnay Day recommended against it. It wasn't proper," he said.
"Institutions had lost their appetite is what they said."

Although violence, in which 73 Arabs and Jews died, has since subsided, and Israeli and Palestinian leaders met in Washington in a bid to resolve issues, Kushnir said he did not regret the delay. "They're absolutely right," he said.
The clashes were sparked by Israel's last week opening an entrance to an archaeological tunnel in Jerusalem.
Nechustan would have been the fifth Israeli company to be listed on London's Alternative Investment Market (AIM).

Another Israeli company, Plasson, was due to complete its IPO on the London Stock Exchange on Thursday, and newspaper reports in Israel said it was likely to be successful. Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull, the sponsor, refused to comment.

Meanwhile, three high-tech issues went through smoothly in the United States in the last week. Telecom products maker Orckit Telecommunications went public last Thursday at $16 a share and its price soared to $20-1/4 in the first day of trading.
This week, Comverse Technololgy Ltd raised $100 million in a private placement and Integrated Technology Ltd made an $18 million offering. Both companies make telecommunications products.
In the last year London has begun to develop as an alternative to New York and the depressed Tel Aviv share market as a place for Israeli companies to go public.
But, said Daniel Fuchs, the Israel representative for the London brokerage Astaire & Partners: "Israel was welcomed outside New York because of the peace process."
Last week's violence has raised doubts about whether it can continue, he said.
He denied that European investors are more sensitive to political events. The three recent U.S. IPOs were in technology stocks, he said, and therefore less affected by peace prospects.
"I hope this will not create a crisis but I think the Israeli government should be concerned," Fuchs said.
